history.title: Swap the Front

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

If you can read the word cat, you can already read six more words. You just do not know it yet.

1. Read **Learn One, Read Many** with a grown-up or a partner.
2. Learn the words in **Sound Words**, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Look at the **Families to Know** chart.
4. Sort the cards in **Same Family or Not?**
5. Take **Word Check** — say every word out loud.
6. Lock it in with **Remember the Swap**.
7. Read **Word Questions Kids Ask**.
8. Finish with **Design: A Family Flip Book**.

Your job this week: find two words that rhyme in a book, and say them to somebody. 🔤

history.title: Learn One, Read Many
history.data:
## Learn One, Read Many

Say this **word**: cat.

Now keep the ending and swap the front. Hat. Bat. Mat. Sat. Rat. Pat.

You just read six new words. You did not learn six new words. You learned one **chunk**, and then you swapped the **start**.

That is a word **family**. All the words end with the same **letters** and the same **sound**.

Here is another one. Hop. Mop. Top. Pop. Same ending, new front each time.

Some fronts have two letters that you say fast together. That is a **blend**. Stop. Chop. Shop. Those are in the same family too.

When words end the same way, they **rhyme**. So a family is a group of words that rhyme.

Every family has a **vowel** in it. The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. The vowel sits in the middle and gives the chunk its sound.

Word families are a **pattern**. Once you spot the pattern, reading gets faster, because you stop sounding out every letter.

But here is something true and a bit annoying. Not every word that rhymes looks the same. Say some and hum. They rhyme. They do not match at all. English does that sometimes.

So use your eyes and your ears. Look for the chunk. Then listen to check.

data.title: Remember the Swap
data.instructions: Two cards hold the moves. Look at the example. Make one your own. Then say how it helps.
data.sourceExcerpt: Now keep the ending and swap the front. You learned one chunk, and then you swapped the start. Say some and hum. They rhyme. They do not match at all.

cards.target: Keep the ending and swap the front sound
essentialFacts: Words in a family end with the same letters.
You keep the chunk and change the start.
Learning one chunk lets you read many words.
cards.aiExample: Two hands. Left hand is the front. Right hand is the chunk. Hold the right hand still. Wiggle the left. Cat, hat, bat. Only one hand moves.
cards.mapping: One hand stays still and one moves. That shows which part of the word changes and which part stays put.
cards.scaffoldStarter: My right hand says ____. My left hand says ____, then ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick a chunk for your right hand.
cards.studentPrompt: Show me a swap with your own hands.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How do your hands show what stays the same?

hookFact.text: You just read six new words. You did not learn six new words.

cards.target: Use your eyes, then check with your ears
essentialFacts: Words in a family look the same at the end.
Words that rhyme sound the same at the end.
Some words rhyme without looking alike, like some and hum.
cards.aiExample: Point to your eyes, then to your ears. Eyes first: does the end look the same? Ears second: does the end sound the same? Two checks, in that order.
cards.mapping: Pointing at your eyes and then your ears puts the two checks in order and reminds you that one is not enough on its own.
cards.scaffoldStarter: My eyes see ____. My ears hear ____.
scaffoldSteps: Point at your eyes and look at the ending.
Point at your ears and say it out loud.
coachPrompts: Did your eyes and ears say the same thing?
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why do you need your ears and not just your eyes?

history.title: Word Check

questions.question: Which word is in the same family as cat?
In the word hop, which part is the chunk?
Which word does NOT belong with big, dig and pig?
What do you do to make a new word in the same family?
options: Change the front and keep the ending
Change the ending and keep the front
Change every letter in the whole word
Add a letter to the end of the word
questions.correctAnswer: Change the front and keep the ending

questions.question: Some and hum rhyme, but they look different. What does that tell you?
options: One of the two words must be spelled wrong
Rhyming words always have to look the same
You should only ever trust your eyes
Words can rhyme without matching letters
questions.correctAnswer: Words can rhyme without matching letters

questions.question: Write three words in the -op family.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. Any three of hop, mop, top, pop, cop, stop, chop, shop, drop. All must end with the letters op.

questions.question: Your friend says cot is in the cat family. What would you tell them?
questions.expectedAnswer: It is not. Cat ends with at and cot ends with ot, so the chunks are different. They start the same, but the family comes from the ending.

reflections.text: Which family was easiest for you?
What two words did you find that rhyme?

history.title: Word Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Why do some words break the rule? 🤔
data.answer: English came from lots of languages. The spellings came along too. So a few words look odd. You learn those by heart.

data.question: How many families are there?
data.answer: Lots. But a few dozen cover most short words. Learn those and a whole shelf of books opens up.

data.question: Is rhyming the same as a family? 🎵
data.answer: Almost. Words in a family rhyme. But some words rhyme without matching letters, like some and hum.

data.question: What if I cannot hear the rhyme?
data.answer: Say both words slowly, one after the other. Then say just the ends. It gets easier with practice.

data.question: Do big words have chunks too? 📚
data.answer: Yes! Long words are made of chunks as well. You will break those apart later. It is the same idea.

data.question: Can two letters make one sound?
data.answer: They can. In shop, the s and h make one sound together. In chop, the c and h do the same.

history.title: Design: A Family Flip Book

data.title: A Family Flip Book
data.instructions: Make a flip book with one ending and lots of fronts. Test it on a partner. See how many real words you can make.
data.fitReason: A flip book makes the swap physical: the ending is fixed to the page and only the front moves. Building one is how a first grader proves they know what a family is.

brief.context: Your class has card strips, scissors, markers, and a stapler the teacher will use. Each of you picks one word family to build.
brief.audience: A partner in your class, who will flip it and read every word
brief.drivingQuestion: How many real words can you make from one ending, and how do you know when a flip is not a real word?
brief.seedDirection: Write the ending once, on the big part. Only the little flipping part changes.
lockedLessonFacts: Words in a family end with the same letters.
You keep the chunk and swap the start.
Some fronts are blends, like st or ch.
openQuestions: Which fronts make real words, and which do not?
Do any of your fronts need two letters?
stakeholders: The class library where it will live
criteria: The ending is written once and does not move
At least five fronts that make real words
At least one front that is a blend
Your partner can read every page out loud
constraints: Real words only on the pages
Ask before you use the stapler
brief.deliverable: A flip book that works, plus one sentence you tell the class: your ending, and how many real words you made.

parallelExample.context: A student picked the ending og and kept making words that were not real.
parallelExample.move: He tried every letter in order and said each one out loud to his partner. They kept dog, log, fog, jog and hog, and put the rest aside.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Saying each one out loud to somebody caught the made-up ones fast.

supports.frameStarter: My ending is ____. My fronts are ____. That makes ____ real words.
